details:
**Ides of March assassination**
Caesar was stabbed to death in a meeting of the Senate on March 15, 44 BC, by a conspiracy led by Marcus Junius Brutus and Gaius Cassius Longinus. Tillius Cimber distracted him by pleading for his exiled brother, and Servilius Casca struck the first blow. His wife Calpurnia reportedly dreamed of his death the night before and begged him not to go. Tradition (popularized by Shakespeare) says he spoke "Et tu, Brute?" to Brutus, whom gossip claimed might be his own son. The assassins were defeated by the Second Triumvirate at Philippi in 42 BC, in the Liberators' Civil War.

**Crossing the Rubicon and "alea iacta est"**
In January 49 BC Caesar led his army across the Rubicon, the river marking the border of his province, into Italy. This was an act of treason that started a civil war against Pompey and the Senate's Optimates. He reportedly said "alea iacta est" ("the die is cast"), and his senior legate Titus Labienus defected to Pompey's side.

**Battle of Pharsalus and the death of Pompey**
Caesar's decisive 48 BC victory in Greece over Pompey the Great, which came after Caesar had been forced to retreat at the Battle of Dyrrhachium. Pompey fled to Egypt, where courtiers of the boy-king Ptolemy XIII murdered him. When Pompey's severed head was presented to Caesar, he reportedly wept in disgust and had his rival's remains properly buried.

**First Triumvirate and the Luca Conference**
An informal political alliance formed around 60 BC between Caesar, Pompey, and Marcus Licinius Crassus. At the Luca (Lucca) Conference in 56 BC the three renewed the pact: Pompey and Crassus would run for consul, and in return Caesar's governorship in Gaul was extended by five years. The alliance broke down after Crassus died at Carrhae and Caesar's daughter Julia died.

**Commentaries on the Gallic War (De Bello Gallico)**
Caesar's third-person account of his conquest of Gaul (58–50 BC), which famously opens "All Gaul is divided into three parts." It describes the Gauls, Germans, and Druids, including human sacrifices in which victims were burned inside giant wicker figures. He also wrote the Commentaries on the Civil War, whose third book ends with events in Egypt, as well as lost works such as the Anticato (an attack on Cato the Younger) and the grammatical treatise De Analogia.

**Battle of Alesia and Vercingetorix**
The 52 BC siege that effectively completed Caesar's conquest of Gaul. Caesar trapped the Arverni chieftain Vercingetorix in the hilltop town of Alesia, building one ring of fortifications facing inward to besiege the town and another facing outward to hold off a huge Gallic relief army. Vercingetorix surrendered and was later paraded in Caesar's triumph and executed.

**Capture by pirates**
As a young man Caesar was kidnapped by Cilician pirates. Insulted that they asked a ransom of only 20 talents, he insisted it be raised to 50 and promised them he would crucify them. After the ransom was paid, he raised a fleet, captured them, and had them crucified.

**Cleopatra and the Alexandrian War**
After following Pompey to Egypt, Caesar sided with Cleopatra VII in her dynastic struggle with her brother Ptolemy XIII. He held out in the Siege of Alexandria and defeated Ptolemy at the Battle of the Nile in 47 BC. Cleopatra bore him a son, Caesarion. Displaying Cleopatra's captured sister Arsinoe IV in his triumph backfired, as Roman crowds sympathized with her.

**Pompeia and the Bona Dea scandal**
In 62 BC, while Caesar was Pontifex Maximus, the politician Publius Clodius Pulcher disguised himself as a woman to sneak into the women-only Bona Dea festival held at Caesar's house, allegedly to meet Caesar's wife Pompeia. Caesar divorced her, reportedly saying that "Caesar's wife must be above suspicion."

**Cornelia and Sulla's proscriptions**
Caesar's wife Cornelia was the daughter of Cinna, an enemy of the dictator Sulla, and Caesar had earlier been betrothed to the wealthy Cossutia. When Sulla ordered Caesar to divorce Cornelia he refused and had to go into hiding, until relatives and allies including Mamercus Aemilius Lepidus and Aurelius Cotta won him a pardon. He later gave funeral orations for Cornelia and for his aunt Julia (widow of Marius), claiming that the Julian family was descended from the goddess Venus.

**"Queen of Bithynia"**
A mocking nickname that came from Caesar's long stay at the court of King Nicomedes IV of Bithynia during his youth, which led to persistent rumors of a sexual relationship between them.

**Dictatorship and reforms**
After the civil war Caesar held the office of dictator repeatedly, finally being named "dictator perpetuo" (dictator in perpetuity) in 44 BC. He took the titles "Father of the Fatherland" and Prefect of Morals and enlarged the Senate to about 900 members. He also introduced the Julian calendar.

**Julia, daughter of Caesar**
Caesar's only legitimate child. She married Pompey to cement the First Triumvirate, and her death in childbirth in 54 BC weakened the bond between the two men. Caesar's great-nephew and adopted son Octavian (later Augustus) went on to form the Second Triumvirate.

**Invasions of Britain**
Caesar led expeditions across the English Channel to Britain in 55 and 54 BC. In the second he defeated the British leader Cassivellaunus and imposed tribute, but he never permanently conquered the island.

**"Veni, vidi, vici"**
"I came, I saw, I conquered," Caesar's message to the Senate after his swift victory over Pharnaces II of Pontus at the Battle of Zela in 47 BC.
